newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Producer group sees drought-hit 1997 maize crop.
newsitem.headline: Producer group sees drought-hit 1997 maize crop.

text.p: Hot and dry weather is likely to reduce this year's South African maize crop to between 7.0 million and 7.8 million tonnes, the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said on Monday.
If growing areas do not get widepsread rains soon the final outturn will be even less, it said in a statement.

Nampo chairman Japie Grobler said the country -- which last year experienced a bumper harvest of over 9.5 million tonnes and which the U.S. Agriculture Department earlier this month forecast would produce a similar amount in the new season -- may be forced to import maize.
He said based on surveys carried out by Nampo, average output per hectare in the new crop, which will be harvested from May, will be between 1.8 and 2.0 tonnes per hectare, down from 2.64 last year.
"Therefore we can expected total production of between 7.0 and 7.8 million tonnes, compared with total consumption of 7.6 million tonnes," Grobler said.

"The potential is falling further each week that rains remain scarce and computer models, which in the past have been very accurate, already put forecasts at lower than six million tonnes," Grobler said.
He said some South African parties had earlier, when crop prospects still looked favourable, signed maize provisioning treaties with neighbouring states.
"(If) these treaties are carried out, then maize will definitely have to be imported. The import quantity will depend on the climate over the next two months," Grobler said.
Grobler said although maize plantings for the 1997 season had increased, very hot and dry weather conditions since the beginning of January had irreparably damaged plants.
South Africa's National Crop Estimates Committee said on Friday its first acreage estimate showed plantings had risen to 3.361 million hectares from 3.307 million last year.
Grobler said there was growing concern among consumers about the state of the crop with net prices offered to producers last week rising from around 500 rand a tonne to 550 rand.
"Prices are expected to rise to about 600 rand a tonne this week and will rise further each week that rains remain scarce," Grobler said.
